14630:
When something skids, it slides suddenly and without control, usually sideways or in an unintended direction, because it has lost its grip on the surface beneath it.

The two most important things about skidding are:

  1. It is uncontrolled — the person or thing doesn't want to move that way.
  2. It happens because grip is lost — the surface becomes too slippery to hold on to.

Imagine a car driving on a wet road. The driver presses the brakes hard. Instead of stopping smoothly, the tyres stop spinning but the car keeps moving forward — now sliding across the wet surface, unable to steer or stop properly. The car might swing sideways. The driver is not in control anymore.

That is skidding.

The car skidded on the wet road.

Skidding happens when there is not enough friction (grip) between two surfaces. Common causes:

  • Ice or snow on a road
  • Wet or oily surfaces
  • Loose gravel or sand
  • Braking too hard or too suddenly
  • Turning too fast

Without friction, the wheels (or feet, or any object) cannot "hold" the surface — they just slide across it.

The verb is most commonly used for vehicles, but not only:

  • The car skidded on the icy road and crashed into the barrier.
  • The truck skidded to a stop just before the red light.
  • His feet skidded on the wet kitchen floor.
  • The box skidded across the floor when she pushed it.

This is a very common phrase. It means something was moving and then skidded — lost control briefly — before finally stopping.

  • The bicycle skidded to a stop at the edge of the footpath.

It suggests the stopping was sudden, uncontrolled, and a little alarming.

These three words can feel similar, so here's how they differ:

Slip — usually very brief and sudden. Often used for a person losing their footing in a single moment.

She slipped on the wet floor. (One sudden moment — she lost balance)

Slide — smooth movement along a surface. Can be intentional or gentle. Doesn't always mean loss of control.

Children slide down the playground slide. (Intentional, smooth, enjoyable)

Skid — uncontrolled sideways or forward sliding, usually for vehicles or objects with momentum. Almost always implies something has gone wrong.

The car skidded off the road. (Loss of control, potentially dangerous)

The key feeling of skid is momentum + loss of grip = danger or near-danger.

When a vehicle skids, its tyres drag across the road and leave dark rubber streaks. These are called skid marks. You've likely seen them on roads — long black lines. They are physical evidence that a vehicle skidded at that spot.

"Skid" is also used figuratively to describe something that suddenly and uncontrollably declines:

  • The economy skidded into recession.
  • His career skidded after the scandal.

Here, the idea is the same — something was moving along steadily, then suddenly lost control and went in a bad direction. The word gives the feeling of a sudden, helpless slide downward.

Core meaningTo slide suddenly and without control, usually sideways, due to loss of grip
Most common subjectVehicles (cars, bikes, trucks), but also people and objects
Caused byWet, icy, oily, or loose surfaces; sudden braking or sharp turning
Key feelingLoss of control + momentum + something going wrong
Figurative useA sudden, uncontrolled decline (career, economy, etc.)
A Few Sentences to Fix It in Your Mind

• The motorbike skidded on a patch of oil and fell over.
  • He skidded across the polished marble floor in his socks.
  • She slammed the brakes, and the car skidded sideways before stopping.
  • The sled skidded off the path and into the snow.
  • After the news broke, the company's stock skidded badly.

Each time you read "skid," picture something that had grip, lost it, and slid helplessly — that is always what it means.
14631: A skiff is a small, simple, open boat — the kind a single person can easily handle on their own. Think of it as the most basic, no-frills boat you can imagine: no cabin, no roof, no fancy equipment. Just a lightweight vessel that gets you across the water.

A skiff typically has a flat or nearly flat bottom, which means it sits very shallow in the water rather than cutting deep into it like a sailboat or a ship. Because of this, it doesn't need much water beneath it to float — a few inches to a foot is often enough. This makes it perfect for rivers, lakes, ponds, marshes, and calm coastal areas where the water is too shallow for bigger boats.

It is usually narrow, open from end to end (you can see straight in — there's no covered deck), and light enough that one person can drag it up onto a shore or beach without much effort.

A skiff can be:

  • Rowed with oars (the classic way)
  • Powered by a small outboard motor attached to the back
  • Sailed with a small sail, in some designs
  • Poled — pushed along with a long pole in very shallow water

There's no single "correct" method. The skiff is versatile and straightforward.

The skiff is essentially a working person's boat. Its most common uses are:

  • Fishing — especially in shallow rivers, bays, and lakes. A fisherman can row out quietly, cast a line, and move around easily.
  • Short crossings — getting from one bank of a river to the other, or reaching a small island nearby.
  • As a companion to a larger vessel — bigger ships often carry a small skiff on board (sometimes called a tender) to let sailors row ashore when the ship can't dock directly.
  • General errands on water — in coastal and riverside communities, the skiff was historically the equivalent of a small car: an everyday, practical tool for getting things done.

If you've ever sat in a small rowboat on a lake — a simple, wooden or aluminum boat with two oars and room for two or three people at most — you've essentially been in something very close to a skiff. It's intimate with the water. Because it sits so low and shallow, you can almost touch the surface with your hand over the side. It moves quietly. It's not built for the open ocean or rough seas — it's built for calm, sheltered water where you need something light, simple, and reliable.

A large ocean liner is to a skiff what a truck is to a bicycle.

In Ernest Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea, the old fisherman Santiago goes out alone into the Gulf Stream in a skiff — a small, simple boat he rows by himself. The word captures his solitude and the modest, humble nature of his life perfectly. That image — one old man, one small boat, the vast ocean — is a good one to hold onto when you think of the word.

In some regional British dialects (particularly in northern England and Scotland), skiff can also refer to a light, brief shower — a very slight fall of rain or snow that barely amounts to anything. "There was just a skiff of snow overnight." This usage is relatively rare and regional, so if you encounter the word without a nautical context, this might be what's meant — but in most cases, across most of the English-speaking world, skiff = small boat.

• "He tied the skiff to the dock and walked up to the house."
  • "They crossed the river in a small skiff, taking turns at the oars."
  • "The fisherman's skiff was barely big enough for two men and their gear."

In short: A skiff is a small, flat-bottomed, open boat — light, simple, and suited for calm, shallow water. It's the most elemental form of a boat: just you, a vessel, and the water.
14632:
A skill is the ability to do something well — an ability that you have developed through learning, practice, and experience.

The two most important parts of that definition are "do something well" and "developed." A skill is not just vague potential. It is a real, working ability that you can actually use. And it doesn't come to you naturally at birth — you build it over time.

Examples: cooking, driving, public speaking, writing code, playing chess, negotiating a deal, reading a map — these are all skills.

A skill has three defining characteristics:

1. It is practical.
A skill is always about doing — performing an action, producing a result, handling a situation. Pure knowing is not a skill. You can read twenty books about swimming and know exactly how the arms and legs should move — but that knowledge alone is not a skill. The skill is swimming itself, the ability to actually get in the water and do it.

2. It is learned and developed.
This is what sets a skill apart from a raw, inborn trait. Nobody is born already knowing how to code or negotiate. You acquire a skill through deliberate effort: instruction, repetition, correction, and experience. This also means skills can be taught, improved, and lost if unused.

3. It involves a level of competence — doing it well.
Not every attempt at something counts as having the skill. If someone has never driven a car before and manages to move it three metres, we wouldn't say they have a "driving skill." A skill implies a reliable, reasonably competent ability. The more reliably and expertly you can do something, the stronger your skill in it.

Skills exist on a spectrum from beginner to master.

You might have a basic skill — you can do the thing, but only in straightforward situations and with some effort. Or you might have an advanced skill — you do it quickly, fluently, and in complex situations without much conscious effort.

This is why we talk about someone having "strong" or "weak" skills, being "highly skilled" or "unskilled" at something. Skill is not an on/off switch; it is a measure of how well you can do something.

A person who has taken one cooking class has some cooking skill. A chef who has cooked thousands of dishes over ten years has highly developed cooking skill. The word covers both — but context tells you the degree.

You will often hear skills divided into two broad categories:

Hard skills are technical, specific, and usually measurable. They often relate to a particular job, tool, or domain. Examples: speaking a foreign language, operating machinery, writing software, performing surgery, playing the violin, using accounting software.

Soft skills are interpersonal and behavioural abilities — how you work with others and handle yourself. Examples: communication, leadership, time management, empathy, problem-solving, adaptability.

Both are real skills. The word "soft" doesn't mean less important — in many careers, soft skills are just as valued as technical ones.

The word works naturally in both singular and plural.

  • One skill: "Public speaking is a skill I want to develop." (referring to one specific ability)
  • Multiple skills: "She brought many skills to the team." (a range of abilities)
  • Skills as a collective: "His skills in carpentry are impressive." (here, "skills" refers to the full set of abilities he has within a domain)

When we say someone has "skill" (without an article, uncountable), we mean general competence or mastery — a more abstract quality. "She performed the surgery with great skill." This is about the quality of expertise itself, not listing individual abilities.

When we say someone has "a skill" or "skills" (countable), we're pointing to specific, nameable abilities. "He has a rare skill: the ability to stay calm under pressure."

Both uses are common and correct.

Knowing how "skill" combines with other words will help you use and recognise it naturally:

  • Develop a skill — to build an ability over time through practice
  • Acquire a skill — to gain a new ability (often through training)
  • Hone a skill — to refine and sharpen an already existing ability
  • Master a skill — to reach a very high level of ability
  • Apply a skill — to use an ability in a real situation
  • Transferable skills — abilities learned in one context that are useful in another (e.g., communication skills learned in teaching can be used in business)
  • Skill set — the complete collection of skills a person has
  • Skill gap — when the skills someone has don't match what a job or task requires
  • Core skills / key skills — the most essential abilities in a particular field
  • Life skills — practical abilities needed for everyday adult life (budgeting, cooking, navigating conflict)
Skill vs. Words That Feel Similar

Skill vs. Talent:
Talent suggests a natural, inborn gift — something you were born with. Skill is what you build through effort. Someone might have a talent for music (a natural ear, quick learning) but still need to develop skill (years of practice, technique) to perform well. In everyday speech, people sometimes use the words loosely, but strictly speaking, talent is innate and skill is earned.

Skill vs. Ability:
Ability is broader — it refers to any capacity you have, whether natural or learned. Skill is more specific: it always implies something learned and implies a certain standard of performance. All skills are abilities, but not all abilities are skills. Having good eyesight is an ability, not a skill. Being a skilled archer, though, is a skill.

Skill vs. Knowledge:
Knowledge is what you know in your mind. Skill is what you can do. You need some knowledge to build a skill, but knowledge alone is not enough. The difference: a doctor reading a textbook about surgery gains knowledge; a doctor who has performed hundreds of operations has skill.

Skill vs. Experience:
Experience is time spent doing something. Skill is what you've actually built as a result. Ten years of experience doesn't automatically mean ten years of skill growth — it depends on whether you were learning and improving. Experience and skill often go together, but they aren't the same thing.

"Skill" is one of the most practically important words in any language because it names something central to human achievement. It captures the idea that most valuable human capabilities are not accidents of birth — they are built. That framing carries a quiet but powerful implication: almost any skill, with enough time and the right effort, can be developed by almost anyone.

When you understand the word deeply, you see it used this way constantly — in education, hiring, sports, art, medicine, and everyday conversation — always pointing to that same core idea: a real, developed ability to do something well.
14633:
Before anything else, here's the one idea that ties all meanings of "skim" together:

To move over or deal with something quickly, lightly, and at the surface — without going deep.

Hold onto this idea. You'll see it at work in every meaning below.
Meaning 1: To Remove Something Floating on Top of a Liquid

When something lighter floats to the surface of a liquid, you can scoop it off with a spoon or ladle. That act is called skimming.

  • A cook skims the fat off chicken soup. The fat rises to the top, and they remove it.
  • Farmers used to skim cream off fresh milk. Cream is lighter than milk, so it floats up — and they'd scoop it away.
  • A chef skims the grey foam off a boiling stock to make it clearer.

The key point: you're only touching the topmost layer. You're not disturbing the liquid below — just removing what's right at the surface.

This is where the term "skim milk" (or "skimmed milk") comes from — it's milk that has had its cream skimmed off, making it lower in fat.
Meaning 2: To Move Quickly and Lightly Over a Surface, Barely Touching It

Here, "skim" describes a type of movement — fast, light, almost gliding, with the least possible contact with the surface below.

  • When you throw a flat stone sideways over a lake, it skims across the water — bouncing several times before finally sinking.
  • A swallow skims the surface of a pond when hunting insects — flying so low its beak barely touches the water.
  • A speedboat skims across the sea — moving so fast it almost floats on top rather than cutting through.
  • The helicopter skimmed the rooftops — flying dangerously low, just barely clearing them.

The movement is always fast and light — never slow, heavy, or deep. The object barely makes contact; it grazes the surface.
Meaning 3: To Read Something Quickly Without Reading Every Word

This is probably the most common use of "skim" in everyday life. When you skim a piece of writing, you don't read it carefully and completely. Instead, you move your eyes quickly through it, catching only the main points — headings, the first sentence of paragraphs, key words — and skipping the rest.

You skim when:

  • You're in a hurry and can't read the whole thing
  • You want a rough idea of what a text is about before deciding whether to read it fully
  • You're looking for one specific piece of information and don't want to read everything
  • You already know the subject well and just want to check the content

Examples:

  • "I didn't have time to read the whole report, so I just skimmed it."
  • "She skimmed through the contract before signing."
  • "He skimmed the chapter and missed the important details buried in the middle."

Important: skimming gives you a surface-level understanding. You get a general idea, but not the depth you'd get from careful reading. It's fast and convenient, but you trade depth for speed.
Meaning 4: To Steal Small Amounts Gradually and Secretly

"Skim" (or "skimming") is also used to describe a type of quiet, gradual theft — taking a little at a time, usually from money or financial transactions, in a way that's hard to notice.

  • A dishonest cashier might skim money from the register — taking a little cash each day over months.
  • Criminals skim credit card data using hidden devices that secretly copy your card's information when you swipe it.

The idea here echoes meaning 1: you're only taking from the top, in small amounts, without making it obvious.

Skim through (something)
To go through a book, document, or article quickly without reading it in full.
"She skimmed through her notes the night before the exam."

Skim over (something)
This phrase is used in two related ways:

  • Physically: to pass lightly over a surface
    "The bird skimmed over the lake."
  • Figuratively: to deal with a topic too briefly, without enough depth
    "The teacher skimmed over the chapter and left students confused."

Skim the surface (of something)
To barely begin exploring something — to touch on it only superficially, not go into real depth. This phrase often signals that something could be explored much more deeply, but hasn't been.
"This short video only skims the surface of quantum physics."
"In one hour, we can barely skim the surface of what Shakespeare wrote."
Why All the Meanings Are the Same at Heart

Look at how the core idea of lightness, speed, and surface-level contact runs through every single meaning:

MeaningWhat stays at the surface
Removing fat from soupYou only touch the top layer, not the liquid below
Stone bouncing on waterIt barely touches the surface, doesn't sink
Reading quicklyYour mind moves fast, doesn't go deep into meaning
Taking small amountsYou take only the "top" — small, unnoticed amounts

Whenever someone says "skim," they're talking about something that stays shallow. It doesn't penetrate. It doesn't slow down. It grazes, glides, or removes from the top — and moves on.
Quick Test: Can You Feel the Difference?

• He read the report carefully. → He went through every word, understood it deeply.
  • He skimmed the report. → He glanced through it quickly, got the gist, nothing more.
  • The duck swam across the lake. → It was in the water, moving through it.
  • The duck skimmed across the lake. → It barely touched the surface, almost flying.

The contrast always shows up the same way: deep and thorough vs. light and surface-level. "Skim" is always on the lighter, faster, more superficial side.
14634:
To skimp means to use less of something than is really needed or appropriate — less money, less material, less effort, less care — usually to save time or money, but in a way that hurts the quality of the result.

The word almost always signals that the reduction was a bad idea, or at least a stingy one. It's not neutral saving — it's saving in a way you shouldn't.

You will almost always see it followed by "on":

skimp on [something]

This is the standard, natural way the word is used. For example:

  • "Don't skimp on the butter."
  • "He skimped on his preparation."
  • "They skimped on safety measures."

1. Using too little of a physical thing

This is about quantity — putting in less material or ingredient than the job actually requires.

  • "The chef skimped on the cheese, so the pizza tasted bland."
  • "The builder skimped on cement to cut costs, and now the wall has cracks."

The idea here is: a proper, full amount was needed, but someone deliberately used less.

2. Spending too little money

This is about being excessively cheap in a situation where being cheap causes problems.

  • "You shouldn't skimp on a good mattress — you sleep on it every night."
  • "The company skimped on employee training to save money, and now errors are everywhere."

Here, the message is: spending more would have been the right call, but someone chose to spend less.

3. Putting in too little effort or care

This is about cutting corners mentally — not doing something as thoroughly or carefully as it deserves.

  • "He skimped on his essay and got a poor grade."
  • "Don't skimp on research before making a big decision."
  • "She skimped on the instructions, and nobody knew how to assemble the furniture."

Skimp is a mild criticism. When you say someone skimped, you're saying they were stingy or careless in a way that was inappropriate for the situation. It's not a harsh insult, but it does carry a negative judgment.

Compare:

  • "She saved money on the wedding." → Neutral, maybe even smart.
  • "She skimped on the wedding." → Suggests she cut too many corners; it came out poorly.

The difference is whether the reduction was reasonable or whether it crossed a line into unacceptable or noticeably bad quality.

• It doesn't mean simply being careful with money in general. A frugal person who manages their budget wisely is not skimping — skimping implies a specific instance where you gave less than was truly needed.
  • It doesn't mean stealing or cheating — it's more about under-giving or under-doing, not taking something dishonestly.

You'll sometimes hear scrimp used in a similar way, often in the phrase "scrimp and save." Both words suggest cutting back too much, but scrimp tends to suggest personal hardship — someone denying themselves comfort to save money. Skimp tends to suggest denying something to a job, a product, or a situation — giving less than the situation deserves.

  • "She scrimped and saved for years to buy a house." → Personal sacrifice.
  • "They skimped on quality when building the house." → The end result suffered.
How to know you've understood it correctly

If you ever want to use skimp, ask yourself: "Is someone using less than they really should — less than the situation truly calls for — and is the result worse for it?" If yes, skimp fits perfectly.

"Don't skimp on sunscreen." "He skimped on sleep before the exam." "The restaurant skimps on portions."

All of these follow the same logic: a proper amount was deserved, but someone gave less — and it shows.
14635: Skimpy means too little of something — not enough in size, amount, or coverage. It describes things that fall short of what is needed, expected, or proper. Think of it as the feeling you get when you expected more but received noticeably less.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

1. Skimpy clothing (not enough fabric)

When describing clothes, skimpy means very small and revealing — the garment covers very little of the body. This is probably the most common use of the word today.

  • A skimpy bikini leaves most of the body uncovered.
  • She wore a skimpy top that barely reached her waist.
  • The costume was so skimpy that the dancer felt exposed on stage.

The idea is that so little fabric was used that the clothing fails to cover what clothing is usually expected to cover. It's not necessarily bad quality — it's just very, very small.

2. Skimpy amounts or efforts (not enough of something)

When describing quantities, meals, work, explanations, or resources, skimpy means inadequate — there is simply not enough of it.

  • The hotel served a skimpy breakfast — just one slice of toast and half a cup of juice.
  • His skimpy excuse didn't convince anyone.
  • The report was skimpy on details; it barely explained anything.
  • The workers were paid a skimpy wage that wasn't enough to live on.
  • After weeks of exercise, she felt cheated by her skimpy results.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Skimpy is an informal, everyday word. It's the kind of word you'd use in casual conversation, not in a formal essay or legal document.

It almost always carries a slightly negative or critical tone. When someone calls something skimpy, they usually mean it's disappointingly small — something is lacking, something is falling short. There's often a sense that someone cut corners, was cheap, or simply didn't provide enough.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She wore a small dress." — just a neutral description.
  • "She wore a skimpy dress." — signals that the dress was notably tiny, possibly scandalously so.

The word skimpy adds judgment or surprise to the description. It's not just small — it's noticeably, questionably small.

It's important not to confuse skimpy with just small or thin. A small book is not automatically a skimpy book. Skimpy specifically implies falling below a reasonable standard or expectation. Something is skimpy when you look at it and think, "That's really not enough."

Also, skimpy doesn't mean low quality in itself — it means low quantity or low coverage. A skimpy meal might be made of perfectly good food; there's just not enough of it on your plate.
A Range of Examples to Cement It

SituationWhy "skimpy" fits
A tiny swimsuitVery little fabric; reveals a lot
A meal with two bites of foodFar less than expected
A report with only one paragraphInsufficient detail for a serious document
A budget so tight nothing gets doneNot enough money allocated
Proof that barely supports a claimToo little evidence to be convincing
Close Relatives (Synonyms) and How Skimpy Differs

• Meager — similar meaning (not enough), but more formal and serious in tone. You'd see meager in a newspaper editorial; skimpy in everyday chat.
  • Scanty — almost identical to skimpy, but sounds slightly more old-fashioned.
  • Revealing — only captures the clothing sense (showing a lot of skin), but doesn't carry the "not enough" idea in general.
  • Sparse — means thinly spread out; skimpy focuses more on overall smallness.
  • Bare minimum — a phrase that captures the spirit of skimpy but isn't a single word.

Of all these, skimpy is the most vivid and versatile for everyday, informal use across both clothing and quantity.
Skimpy = noticeably and disappointingly too small or too little — whether it's clothing that barely covers you, food that barely fills you, or an explanation that barely informs you.
14636: Skin refers to the outermost covering or layer of something — whether a living body, a fruit, a liquid, or even a digital interface. The common thread across all its meanings is this: skin is what you encounter first on the outside, before you get to what's inside.
Meaning 1: The Outer Covering of the Human or Animal Body

This is the most fundamental and widely used meaning.

Skin is the soft, flexible tissue that covers the entire body of a human or animal. It is the largest organ of the human body. It is what you can see and touch when you look at a person or an animal.

Skin serves several important purposes:

  • It protects the internal organs, muscles, and bones from damage, infection, and harmful things in the environment.
  • It regulates body temperature — for example, by sweating.
  • It senses the world — it can feel touch, pressure, pain, heat, and cold.
  • It acts as a barrier against water loss and germs.

Human skin varies in colour, texture, and thickness across different people and across different parts of the same body. The skin on your eyelids, for example, is very thin and delicate, while the skin on the soles of your feet is much thicker.

"She had smooth, dark skin."
"The cold wind made his skin dry and rough."
"The doctor examined the rash on the patient's skin."
Meaning 2: The Hide or Pelt of an Animal (Removed from the Body)

When an animal's skin is removed from its body — often after the animal has died — it is also called a skin (or sometimes a hide or pelt, depending on the animal and how it is processed).

Animal skins have been used by humans for thousands of years to make clothing, shoes, bags, rugs, and other items. When processed and treated, animal skin becomes leather.

"The trader brought beaver skins to sell at the market."
"They wore cloaks made from animal skins."
"The craftsman used the skin of a goat to make a drum."
Meaning 3: The Outer Covering of a Fruit, Vegetable, or Food

The thin outer layer that covers fruits and vegetables is also called their skin.

You are probably familiar with this meaning: the skin of an apple is the smooth coloured layer on the outside; the skin of a potato is the thin brownish coat that wraps around it. This is also sometimes called the peel (especially for fruits like oranges and bananas), but skin is perfectly natural for most foods.

"She peeled the skin off the apple before eating it."
"Potato skins can be baked and eaten as a snack."
"The grapes had thin, delicate skins."
"Some recipes ask you to remove the skin from the tomatoes."
Meaning 4: A Thin Film or Layer That Forms on the Surface of a Liquid

When certain liquids are heated and then left to cool, or when they begin to dry out, a thin layer forms on top of them. This layer is called a skin.

You have likely seen this happen with hot milk — when it cools, a thin film forms on the surface. The same thing can happen with paint, custard, gravy, or pudding.

"A skin had formed on the top of the hot chocolate."
"Stir the sauce occasionally so a skin doesn't form."
"The old tin of paint had developed a thick skin on top."
Meaning 5: The Outer Surface or Shell of an Object or Structure

Skin can also refer to the outer covering or surface layer of a physical structure or object, especially when that covering is thin relative to what it encloses.

This meaning is used in engineering, construction, and design. For example, an aeroplane has a skin — the thin metal or composite material that covers the outside of the aircraft's frame. A building can have a skin — the external cladding that covers its structural skeleton.

"The aircraft's skin was made of lightweight aluminium alloy."
"Workers repaired the damaged skin of the fuselage."
"The building's glass skin reflected the sky."
"A thin skin of ice covered the surface of the lake."

The last example shows how this sense extends to nature too — a thin layer of ice, dust, or other material covering something can be called its skin.
Meaning 6: A Container Made from Animal Skin (Historical/Traditional)

In older times, and still in some traditional cultures today, bags or pouches made from the skin of animals were used to carry and store liquids such as water or wine. These containers were simply called skins.

"The traveller carried water in a goatskin."
"They filled the skins with wine before the journey."

You may encounter this meaning in historical texts, religious scriptures, or stories set in ancient times.
Meaning 7: A Digital Visual Theme or Cosmetic Overlay (Computing and Gaming)

In modern usage, skin has acquired a popular digital meaning.

In computing and software, a skin is a visual theme that changes the appearance of a program, app, or device without changing how it actually works. It is like a costume for software — the same functions remain, but the colours, buttons, icons, and overall look change.

In video games, a skin is a cosmetic item that changes the appearance of a character, weapon, or other in-game element. Players often purchase or earn skins to make their character look different from the default appearance — but the skin has no effect on the character's abilities or the gameplay itself.

"She downloaded a new skin to change the look of her media player."
"He spent real money on a rare skin for his character in the game."
"The app lets you apply different skins to customise the interface."
Meaning 8: Cigarette Rolling Paper (British Informal Slang)

In informal British English, skin can refer to a cigarette rolling paper — a thin, light paper used to hand-roll cigarettes. This is quite colloquial and regional, and you are most likely to hear it in informal speech in the UK.

"Have you got a skin I can use?"
Important Phrases and Expressions Using "Skin"

Because skin is such a fundamental part of human experience, the word appears in many common phrases and idioms. These are fixed expressions whose meanings go beyond the literal meaning of the word.

"By the skin of one's teeth"
This means barely or only just. If you escape something "by the skin of your teeth," you escaped with the smallest possible margin — it was extremely close.

"She passed the exam by the skin of her teeth."

"Get under someone's skin"
This means to irritate or bother someone deeply, or alternatively, to affect someone emotionally in a way that is hard to ignore.

"His constant criticism really got under her skin."
"That song has really gotten under my skin — I can't stop thinking about it."

"Save one's skin"
To save oneself from danger, punishment, or a difficult situation.

"He lied to the police just to save his own skin."

"Skin and bones"
Used to describe someone or something that is extremely thin or underweight.

"After weeks of illness, he was nothing but skin and bones."

"In one's own skin" / "Comfortable in one's own skin"
To be at ease with who you are — your identity, your body, your personality.

"It took her years to feel comfortable in her own skin."

"It's no skin off my nose" (or "off my back")
This means that something does not affect you personally — you don't care either way, because there is no cost to you.

"If he wants to quit, it's no skin off my nose."

"Skin in the game"
To have a personal stake in an outcome — to be personally affected by the result of a situation, usually because you have invested something (money, effort, reputation) into it.

"She has real skin in the game — she invested her life savings into the company."

"Beauty is only skin deep"
A saying that means outward appearance is superficial and does not reflect a person's true character or worth.

"Thick skin" / "Thin skin" (used as noun phrases)
To have thick skin means to be able to handle criticism, insults, or hardship without being badly affected.
To have thin skin means to be easily hurt or offended.

"You need thick skin to work in politics."
"She has thin skin — even a small comment upsets her."
Quick Summary of All Senses

• On a person or animal → the natural outer tissue covering the body.
  • On an animal (removed) → its hide or pelt, used to make leather or clothing.
  • On a fruit or vegetable → its thin outer covering (like apple skin, potato skin).
  • On a liquid → a thin film that forms on the surface as it cools or dries.
  • On a structure or object → the thin outer surface or shell (like an aircraft's skin, or ice skin on a lake).
  • Historical containers → pouches or bags made from animal hides.
  • In computing and gaming → a visual theme or cosmetic overlay that changes appearance.
  • British slang → a cigarette rolling paper.
14637: When "skin" is used as a verb, the central idea is almost always about removing or damaging an outer covering — whether that's the hide of an animal, the peel of a fruit, or the surface layer of your body. From this core idea, the word branches out into several related and figurative uses.
Meaning 1: To Remove the Skin or Outer Layer of Something

This is the most literal meaning. It simply means to peel off or strip away the outer covering of an animal, a fruit, or a vegetable.

With animals:

"The hunter skinned the rabbit before cooking it."

This means the hunter removed the animal's hide (its outer skin/fur) from its body. Hunters, farmers, and butchers do this after an animal is killed, either to prepare the meat for eating or to keep the hide/fur for other uses.

With food:

"She skinned the tomatoes by dipping them in hot water first."

Here it means she removed the thin outer peel of the tomatoes. You might also hear "peel" used for fruits and vegetables, but "skin" is very natural here too.

"The recipe asks you to skin the almonds."

This means to remove the thin brown coating around the almonds.

The logic: Just as a noun, "skin" is the outer layer. As a verb, "to skin" = to take that layer away.
Meaning 2: To Scrape or Graze the Skin Off a Part of Your Body

This is extremely common in everyday speech. It means you accidentally scraped your skin against a hard surface, causing the top layer of your skin to get rubbed off. This usually results in a small wound — a little blood, a sting, and redness.

"I fell off my bike and skinned my knee."

The knee scraped against the road. The top layer of skin got rubbed off.

"He skinned his elbow climbing over the wall."

"She tripped and skinned both her palms."

Notice that this meaning is almost always about accidental injury. You don't do it on purpose. The object is usually a body part: your knee, elbow, knuckle, shin, or palm. These are all parts of the body that people commonly scrape in everyday accidents.
Meaning 3: To Cheat or Swindle Someone (Informal)

In informal, mostly older usage, "to skin someone" means to cheat them out of their money — to take advantage of them unfairly in a deal or transaction. The image is of stripping someone of what they have, like stripping an animal of its skin — leaving them with nothing.

"That dishonest mechanic really skinned me — he charged ₹10,000 for a job worth ₹1,000."

"Be careful at that market. If you're not sharp, the vendors will skin you alive."

This meaning is relatively informal and not heard in formal writing. You are more likely to come across it in older books, films, or conversations where someone is warning you about being cheated.
Meaning 4: To Beat Someone Completely / To Defeat Easily (Informal)

In casual British and American English, "to skin" someone can mean to defeat them thoroughly or outclass them completely in a game, competition, or contest.

"Our team skinned them 7–0."

"She skinned all the other contestants in the quiz."

This sense is not extremely common, but you will encounter it in sports commentary and casual talk.
Meaning 5: To Easily Get Past Someone (Sports, Especially British Football)

In British sports language — particularly in football (soccer) — "to skin" a player means to get past a defender so skillfully and easily that you make them look slow or helpless. It's used admiringly.

"He just skinned two defenders and scored."

"She skinned the left back and crossed the ball into the box."

The image here is of moving so fast and fluidly that you seem to slip right past the defender the way a knife slips through skin. This meaning is very common in football commentary in Britain.
Meaning 6: To Apply a "Skin" to Software or a Device (Tech/Gaming)

In computing and gaming, a "skin" is a custom visual theme — a set of graphics that changes how an app, game character, or interface looks, without changing how it works. So "to skin" something means to apply such a visual theme or redesign to it.

"You can skin the media player to make it look completely different."

"He skinned his phone to look like it runs a different operating system."

"The game lets you skin your character with rare outfits."

This is a modern, digital-age meaning, very common in gaming communities and among tech-savvy users. When gamers buy or earn a "skin" for their weapon or character, and then apply it, they are "skinning" that item.
Important Phrases and Expressions Using "Skin" as a Verb

"Skin someone alive"

This is a vivid and dramatic expression. Literally, it would mean to remove someone's skin while they are still alive — an ancient form of extreme punishment. But in everyday modern use, it is a hyperbolic way to say you will punish someone very severely, or that you are extremely angry at them. Nobody actually means they will do this.

"If you break my phone, I will skin you alive."

"My mother will skin me alive if I come home this late."

It simply means: "I/she will be furious and there will be serious consequences." It's an exaggeration used for emphasis and dramatic effect.

"There's more than one way to skin a cat"

This is a well-known idiom (a fixed phrase with a figurative meaning). It means there are many different methods or approaches to accomplish the same goal. The "cat" here is not taken literally at all — it is simply an old, colorful expression.

"I know the front door is locked, but there's more than one way to skin a cat — let's try the back entrance."

The point is: don't get stuck on one approach. If one way doesn't work, try another.
A Quick Summary of All Uses

• Skin an animal or food → remove its outer covering physically
  • Skin your knee / elbow / palm → accidentally scrape the skin off a body part
  • Skin someone (old informal) → cheat them out of money
  • Skin a team / opponent (informal) → defeat them completely
  • Skin a defender (sports) → get past them with ease and skill
  • Skin an app / character / device (tech/gaming) → apply a custom visual theme
  • Skin someone alive (expression) → threaten severe punishment; express extreme anger
  • More than one way to skin a cat (idiom) → multiple approaches to a problem
How to Recognize Which Meaning Is Being Used

The context does almost all the work:

  • If someone is hunting, cooking, or in a kitchen → it's about removing an outer covering
  • If someone fell or tripped → it's about scraping a body part
  • If it's about a business deal or money → it's the "cheat" meaning
  • If it's about a game or competition → it's about dominating or defeating
  • If it's British sports commentary → it's about getting past a defender
  • If it's about computers, games, or apps → it's about applying a visual theme
  • "Skin alive" or "skin me/you/him alive" → it's the anger/punishment expression

The word "skin" as a verb is remarkably flexible, but once you understand that all its uses share the idea of stripping away a surface, slipping past something, or completely overpowering something, every use will feel natural and logical to you.
14638:
"Skin and bones" means extremely thin or underweight — so thin that a person (or animal) looks like there is nothing on their body except skin covering their skeleton. It suggests a severe lack of body weight, to the point where it looks unhealthy or alarming.

Think of it literally for a moment: if someone has only skin and bones, it means all the flesh, muscle, and fat in between have disappeared. That visual image is exactly what the idiom captures.
How It Sounds in a Sentence

The idiom is almost always used with the verb "be" or "become", and it's paired with the word "nothing but" or "just" to make it hit harder:

  • "She was nothing but skin and bones after her long illness."
  • "The stray dog was just skin and bones when we found it."
  • "He's been working so hard and not eating — he's turned into skin and bones."
  • "After months of travelling without proper food, I became skin and bones."

The phrase "nothing but skin and bones" is the most classic and natural way to use this idiom. You'll hear it this way very frequently.
The Tone and Feeling Behind It

This idiom carries a tone of concern, worry, or sympathy. When someone says another person is "skin and bones," they are not being playful or complimentary. They are expressing that the person looks dangerously thin — often because of illness, starvation, stress, grief, or neglect.

It is not an insult in the rude sense, but it is definitely not a neutral observation either. It signals that something is wrong or that the person needs care and nourishment.

For example:

  • "Look at her — she's nothing but skin and bones. Someone needs to make sure she's eating properly."

Here, the speaker is worried, not mocking.
Can It Be Used for Animals Too?

Yes, absolutely. This idiom applies equally well to animals — often stray or neglected ones:

  • "The rescue team found the horse in an abandoned barn, skin and bones, barely able to stand."
  • "My cat was skin and bones when I adopted her from the shelter."
Origin — Where Did It Come From?

The idiom has been in the English language for centuries. The idea of describing extreme thinness by referencing just "skin" and "bones" is so natural and visual that it developed independently across many cultures and languages. In English, written records of this phrase go back to at least the 16th and 17th centuries.

It is a universal concept: in almost every language, extreme thinness is described by saying that only the outer layer (skin) and the inner frame (bones) remain, with nothing in between. English simply made this into a fixed expression.
Literal vs. Figurative

It is important to understand that this is always used figuratively in modern English — nobody means it completely literally (as in, a person has zero muscle or fat at all). It is an exaggeration (a hyperbole) used to emphasize just how thin someone appears.

This is very common in English idioms: they take a vivid, extreme image and use it to describe a real-world situation with emotional punch.
Common Variations and Related Forms

You may also encounter these slightly different versions — they all mean the same thing:

  • "All skin and bones" — "He's all skin and bones these days."
  • "Nothing but skin and bones" — the most common form.
  • "Just skin and bones" — "She looks just skin and bones."
  • "A bag of bones" — a closely related idiom, same meaning, also very common.
  • "Skin-and-bones" (used as a compound adjective before a noun) — "He was a skin-and-bones figure standing in the doorway."
Similar Idioms With the Same Meaning

If you want to say the same thing in a different way, here are related expressions in English:

  • "A bag of bones" — very common, almost identical in meaning and tone.
  • "Thin as a rake" (British English) — comparing thinness to a garden rake, which is very narrow.
  • "Thin as a rail" — comparing to a thin metal or wooden rail.
  • "Wafer-thin" — extremely thin, though this one is used more for objects than people.
What It Is NOT

It's worth being clear about what this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean someone is simply slim or lean in a healthy way. If someone is fit and athletic, you would not say they are "skin and bones." That would actually sound offensive and inaccurate.
  • It is not a compliment. In Western culture today, being very thin is sometimes seen as desirable, but this idiom is never used as praise — it always suggests something is wrong.
  • It does not apply to objects or abstract things. You would not say "the company is skin and bones" (unless you are using very unusual metaphorical language). It is used for people and animals.
Quick Summary

MeaningExtremely thin and underweight, to an alarming degree
Used forPeople and animals
ToneConcern, worry, sympathy
Most common form"Nothing but skin and bones"
Type of languageInformal / conversational
Literally true?No — it's a hyperbole (exaggeration) for effect
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

Imagine a family member who has been very sick for months and has lost a lot of weight. When a relative visits after a long time, they might say:

"Oh my goodness — look at him. He's nothing but skin and bones. We need to get some good food into him right away."

That sentence captures everything: the visual shock of extreme thinness, the emotional concern, and the caring impulse to help. That is "skin and bones" in its full, natural use.
14639: A skinflint is a person who is extremely unwilling to spend money — someone so stingy and tight-fisted that they will go to unreasonable lengths to avoid parting with even the smallest amount of cash. It is always used as an insult or a mockery.
Going Deeper: What Makes Someone a Skinflint?

The word doesn't just describe someone who is careful with money. It describes someone whose reluctance to spend has crossed into selfishness and near-obsession. A skinflint isn't merely thrifty — they are someone whose grip on their money is so tight that it embarrasses or harms the people around them.

Here's the crucial distinction:

  • A frugal person avoids unnecessary spending to live wisely within their means. This is considered a virtue.
  • A skinflint refuses to spend even when it is clearly reasonable, expected, or fair to do so. This is considered a flaw — often a shameful one.

A skinflint at a restaurant might calculate every person's share of the bill down to the last rupee to avoid paying even a little more than what's "theirs." A skinflint employer might make employees wait weeks for reimbursements they are owed. A skinflint relative might give a child a used, broken toy as a birthday gift to save money. The behavior isn't born out of genuine hardship — it comes from an obsessive, almost irrational attachment to holding onto money.

What truly defines a skinflint is not just the action but the mindset. A skinflint prioritises keeping their money over:

  • Generosity — They resist giving gifts, tips, donations, or any kind of financial help to others, even when it would cost them very little.
  • Fairness — They avoid paying their fair share in group situations, letting others quietly absorb costs they should contribute to.
  • Comfort and dignity — They may deprive not just others but sometimes even themselves of reasonable comforts, to an almost comical or pitiable degree.
  • Relationships — Their stinginess often strains friendships, family ties, and professional respect, because people around them feel taken advantage of.

Skinflint is an informal, colloquial word. When someone is called a skinflint, there is contempt and mockery in the air — sometimes mixed with mild humour. It's the kind of word used behind someone's back, or said to their face in a moment of frustration or teasing. It is not a neutral, clinical description. It carries a clear judgment: this person is unacceptably cheap, and it reflects poorly on their character.

It sits comfortably alongside words like miser, cheapskate, penny-pincher, tightwad, and Scrooge (the last one being a reference to the famous fictional character Ebenezer Scrooge from Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol, who is perhaps the most well-known portrait of this type of person in all of literature).
How It Differs From Similar Words

WordNuance
  • Miser leans toward someone who hoards money obsessively, almost like a psychological condition — they derive a strange pleasure from accumulation. A skinflint and a miser overlap greatly, but "miser" feels slightly more formal and literary.
  • Cheapskate is more casual and focuses specifically on someone who avoids paying their fair share in everyday situations (like splitting a bill). A skinflint is a broader, deeper kind of cheapness.
  • Penny-pincher is milder in tone — it can even be used semi-affectionately. A skinflint is harsher and implies the behaviour has become offensive or unacceptable.
  • Tightwad is similarly informal and emphasises someone who holds onto money as if physically clutching it. Close to skinflint but slightly less sharp in tone.

A skinflint is probably the most vivid and cutting of these everyday synonyms.

1. My landlord is such a skinflint that he refused to fix the broken tap for eight months because he didn't want to pay the plumber.
  2. Don't invite him to dinner — he's a notorious skinflint who always "forgets" his wallet.
  3. She worked for that skinflint for years and never once got a raise, even as the company made record profits.
  4. For a man worth crores, he acted like a complete skinflint, bargaining over ten-rupee coins at the vegetable market.
  5. I've met frugal people, but he's something else entirely — an absolute skinflint who won't even offer guests a glass of water.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

A skinflint is a person who is unreasonably, selfishly, and often embarrassingly stingy with money — not because they are poor, but because they are deeply reluctant to let go of what they have, even when fairness or basic generosity calls for it. The word is informal, contemptuous, and always critical. It paints a picture of someone whose tightness with money has become a character flaw visible and irritating to everyone around them.
